## Abstract

Background: The skin is the largest organ and is subject to the greatest exposure to outside elements throughout one׳s lifetime. Current data by the American Academy of Dermatology suggests that approximately ten people die each hour worldwide due to skin related conditions. Cancers such as melanoma are growths that originate in the epidermis. Therefore, an accurate and non-invasive method to estimate skin constitutive elements can play an important clinical role in detecting the early onset of skin tumors. It can also serve as a valuable tool for research and development in cosmetics and pharmaceuticals in general.

Methods: In our prior work, we developed a method that combined a physics-based model of human skin with machine learning and Hyperspectral imaging to non-invasively estimate physiological skin parameters, including melanosomes, collagen, oxygen saturation, and blood volume. In this work, we extend that model to also estimate skin thickness. Moreover, for the first time, we develop a protocol to test our methodology for skin thickness estimation using Ultrasound to acquire a gold standard dataset.

Results: We tested our methodology for skin thickness estimation on a dataset of 48 Hyperspectral signatures obtained in vivo from six patients under IRB at Johns Hopkins Hospital. We found mean absolute errors on the order of the Ultrasound resolution (i.e., our gold standard).

Discussion: This is the first study of its kind to validate skin thickness estimates using a gold standard. Our preliminary results constitute a proof-of-concept that hyperspectral-based methods can accurately and non-invasively estimate skin thickness in clinical settings.

Keywords: Hyperspectral signatures; Machine learning regression; Skin thickness; Ultrasound.

Advancements in AI have introduced more precise and efficient methods for skin type assessment. Chang et al. explored the use of spectral data combined with a CNN model to classify skin types based on the Fitzpatrick scale, showcasing the potential of AI in utilizing spectral measurements, with an accuracy rate of 92.59% [12]. In contrast, Borade et al. focused on image-based analysis, employing a hybrid model of wavelet scattering networks and ResNet, which demonstrated high accuracy in classifying dry and oily skin types, even with limited datasets [13]. Building on this, Kothari et al. applied an enhanced CNN model to high-resolution facial images, extracting features such as texture and oiliness to achieve consistent and reliable skin type classifications [14].

Skin thickness is crucial for both pathological evaluations and aesthetic treatments, particularly for treatments such as rejuvenating lasers and fillers designed to restore a fuller and thicker appearance. AI-based noninvasive estimation methods provide a promising alternative to traditional techniques that typically rely on skin biopsies. A model utilizing machine learning and hyperspectral imaging was proposed for the noninvasive estimation of human skin thickness, demonstrating accuracy comparable to ultrasound, the clinical gold standard [15]. It successfully estimated the thickness of five skin layers and four dermal layers across various anatomical locations, including the dorsal forearm, upper inner arm, calf, and cheek, offering a promising tool for precise and noninvasive skin analysis.

## From Aesthetic Concerns to Diseases: AI in Diagnosis

### Vitiligo

Vitiligo, although a benign condition, can significantly impact patients’ quality of life and impose considerable psychosocial stress, particularly when lesions are visible on areas such as the face, neck, and hands. While the diagnosis of vitiligo is relatively straightforward, its assessment poses challenges such as variability in lesion number, size, location, shape, and degree of depigmentation, especially when considering post-treatment repigmentation.

Accurate identification and evaluation of lesion size and pigmentation changes are essential for monitoring disease progression and assessing therapeutic outcomes. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.6 Visibility

Verification of visibility relative to observations for UK and Darwin NWP tests shows consistently improved performance of RAL3.0 (Fig. 2). In contrast, tropical Africa and South-East Asia NWP results show a marked reduction in visibility forecast skill in RAL3.0 relative to RAL2-T. This is linked to the change from using a global constant value for aerosol concentrations in the visibility diagnostic to use of climatological aerosols with more regional variability (e.g. relatively increased aerosol over the SE Asia region). In practice, use of a global constant in RAL2-T meant that while summary scores were apparently acceptable, the treatment of aerosol was inadequate as a forecasting tool (e.g. rarely predicting low-visibility events). In RAL3, the move to more realistic geographical distributions has tended to increase both the probability of detection of lower visibility categories and the probability of false detection (e.g. now tending to predict low-visibility events too frequently), noting also the relatively sparse network of observing stations.
